text: A quantum circuit doesn't hand you an answer — it hands you a dictionary of bitstring counts. Turning that into the number your business logic actually needs is entirely classical code, and it's where a surprising number of production bugs hide.

We'll convert real measurement counts into an expectation value by hand, see why a standard error has to travel alongside that value every time, and walk through the three post-processing bugs that are easiest to ship without anyone noticing.

Here's the conversion, worked in full. A thousand-shot measurement comes back as six hundred twelve zeros and three hundred eighty-eight ones. Using the standard convention — zero maps to plus one, one maps to minus one — the expectation value is the counts-weighted average: zero point two two four. Get that eigenvalue mapping backwards, and every downstream number has its sign flipped, silently, with no error thrown anywhere in the pipeline.
This is real output of exactly that kind of conversion, straight from IBM Quantum's documentation — expectation values computed across six different observables from one circuit's measurement counts.

And here's why the error bar matters so much: a real measured result from IBM's own hardware, showing exactly the kind of noise that gets mistaken for signal when nobody reports a standard error. A thousand shots gives roughly a three percent standard error — report a bare number with no uncertainty attached, and you invite exactly this mistake.

This is where the raw counts actually come from before any of this post-processing runs — a real Amazon Braket quantum task detail page, showing status, shot count, and where the results land. Everything past this point is classical code you write and test like any other code.
Next lesson chains both classical halves together — data preparation going in, result aggregation coming out — into one complete, tested pipeline.
